title: Desktop and Phone Companion Plan
eyebrow: Plan for approval · nothing built yet
approval: Design approved: desktop and phone companion

short.lead: Every session has two views on both your PC and your phone. One is the real terminal. The other is a Visual view that looks like the Claude app: chat bubbles, one-tap question cards, the pages and pictures Claude made, and a plain reason for every step. Both views show the same live session at once, across all your accounts, with no account switching. It is built around how your brain works: one thing at a time, a picture for everything, a reason for everything, and nothing that moves unless you asked.
short.hint: Tap an item to see what it creates and what it needs from you.

changes: keep
What already exists, and what this plan reuses
Nothing is built yet; this plan grows the first design rather than starting again.

Today the repository holds only documents. The first design page, docs/plans/router-prototype.html, planned a Windows board that finds every session in three account folders (you have four) and groups them by project. It was never approved, so nothing here throws work away. The previous version of this plan gave the phone only a terminal and offered a chat view as an either-or choice; this version gives both devices both views. This plan keeps that page's session finder, the account slots, the board, the first-run walkthrough and the calm design. It changes two things: it settles that page's open stack question by making the app an installable .exe, and it runs sessions inside the app instead of opening Windows Terminal. The first page's other two questions carry over with their suggested answers. The layout question keeps the board. The question about how your accounts are set up today is settled by the app checking for itself on first launch. Tell me in your reply if you want either changed. Claude Code itself, its account folders and its session files are used exactly as they are; the router only reads the session files, except when you tap to move a conversation to another account.

changes: chg
Any number of accounts
Four accounts are ready out of the box, and you can add or remove as many as you like.
The first design had exactly three fixed slots: Main, Work and Spare.
Four slots to start, named Main, Work, Spare and Extra, with an Add account button and no upper limit.

Each account is one folder. Slot one is your normal folder, %USERPROFILE%\.claude. Every other slot uses .claude-account2, .claude-account3 and so on in your user folder. The first launch finds every folder that already exists, so your four accounts show without any setup. Add account makes the next folder; Claude asks you to sign in to it once, the first time it starts a session there. Each account gets its own colour and name, and you can rename it. The account router and the phone treat every account the same way, however many you have.
chg
Start and resume run inside the app
Sessions open in a terminal inside EdensRouter instead of a separate window.
New session or Resume opens Windows Terminal in the project folder. Only the PC can see that window.
New session or Resume opens a terminal tab inside EdensRouter. The app keeps it running, so the phone can watch it and type into it too.

The terminal host is the new heart of the app. It runs the real claude command for the account you picked. A hidden terminal does this, using node-pty, the open-source library VS Code uses. The app shows that terminal with xterm.js, VS Code's terminal display. Because the app owns the session, closing a tab hides it without stopping it, and a phone can attach to it at any time. Nothing about Claude itself changes: it is the same command you run by hand, signed in with that account's own folder.
new
Visual view: the Claude app look, live
Chat bubbles, question cards, pages and pictures, and a reason for every step, on PC and phone.

The Visual view shows the same session as the terminal, drawn the way the Claude app draws it. Your messages and Claude's replies are bubbles. Each thing Claude does is a card: an edit shows the file and the lines changed, and tapping it opens the change; a command shows its result in one line, with the full output folded away until you ask. Every card carries a Why line, taken from what Claude said just before it acted, so you always know the reason. When Claude asks a question or asks permission, it becomes a card with one big button per answer, its suggestion marked, and a box for your own answer. Pages, diagrams and pictures Claude makes (HTML, SVG, PNG, JPG and Markdown files) show inside the conversation, and you tap them to open full size. A link to a claude.ai artifact shows as a card that opens it in your browser, because those pages need your claude.ai sign-in. Claude's task list sits at the top as a Now strip, so you can see which step it is on.
The terminal shows everything as scrolling text, and questions are numbered lists you answer with arrow keys.
A Visual view of every session, on both devices, beside the terminal.
You see what is happening and why at a glance, and answer with one tap.

changes.alt: Visual view mock-up. At the top, a Now strip with five steps, two done in green. Below it, chat bubbles, an edit card with a Why line, a folded test result and a chart page Claude made. At the bottom, an orange question card with three answer buttons, then a message box.

changes: new
How both views stay in step
The terminal is the real thing; the Visual view is drawn from Claude's own record of the session.

Claude Code writes every message and tool call into the session's transcript file as it works. I checked this on this very session: its transcript held 89 Claude messages and 59 tool calls, each as structured data, while the session was still running. The router reads that file as it grows and draws the Visual view from it. When you tap an answer or send a message in the Visual view, the router types it into the hidden terminal as the same keys you would press, so Claude sees exactly what it would see from the keyboard. Nothing about Claude changes, and every terminal feature keeps working.
Only the terminal shows a session.
One live session that both views read, and both views can answer.
Switch views any time without losing your place.

changes.alt: Diagram. Claude, in a hidden terminal, sends its screen to the Terminal view and writes the transcript file. The transcript file feeds the Visual view. A dashed orange arrow runs from the Visual view back to Claude: your tap or message, sent as the keys you would press.
changes.caption: How one session feeds both views. Orange is the path your own input takes.

changes: new
Built around ADHD and autism
Seven features that cut noise, show progress and give a reason for everything.

Needs-you list: one list, across every project and account, of sessions waiting for you, newest first, with a phone notification when one is added. Focus card: when Claude asks something, the question fills the screen with big answer buttons, and nothing else moves until you answer or put it aside. Now strip: Claude's task list as a row of steps, done ones in green, so progress is visible. Why line: every action card says why Claude did it. Calm scrolling: the view never jumps while you read; new messages wait behind a New below button, long output stays folded, and a reduce-motion setting turns animation off. Where-you-were card: opening a session shows its goal and the last thing done, taken from the session's title and Claude's last message. Pages shelf: every page, diagram and picture Claude has made in a project, in one place. Colours keep one meaning everywhere: orange means Claude needs you, green means done, and each account and project keeps its own colour.
Sessions are walls of text, and a waiting question is easy to miss.
A calm, visual layer over every session.
You know what needs you, what is happening and why, without reading everything.

changes.alt: Two phone screens: a Needs-you list with two orange waiting sessions, one working session and one done today; and a session showing a Where you were card above a single orange question card with big answer buttons
changes.caption: Mock-up: the Needs-you list, and a question as a focus card.

changes: new
Account router: never switch accounts
Every project opens on the right account, and moves to another account with one tap when it has to.

When you open a project, the router starts Claude with that project's last-used account, by pointing CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (the setting that tells Claude which account folder to use) at that account's folder. You never sign out or in. If Claude prints its usage-limit message, the router shows one button: Continue on Spare (or whichever account has room). Tapping it copies that session's transcript file into the other account's folder and resumes it there with claude --resume, so the conversation carries on with its full history. Your sign-ins are never copied or shared between accounts.
Each account lives in its own folder, and moving work between them means signing out and in by hand.
A router that remembers each project's account and moves a conversation in one tap.
You pick up any project on any device without thinking about accounts.

changes.alt: Four-step flow: you open plunderspell on Work, Work is out of usage, you tap Continue on Spare, and the same conversation continues on Spare
changes.caption: How a conversation moves to another account. Step four has not been tried yet, because it needs two signed-in accounts on your PC.

changes: new
Android companion app
Everything the PC app does, on your phone.

The phone app uses the same screens as the PC, built from the same code, so the two never drift apart. Every session has the same Terminal and Visual switch. In the terminal, a row of keys a phone keyboard lacks sits under a large text box: Esc, up, down and Enter. While the app is open or running in the background, it keeps its link to the PC and shows a notification when a session lands on the Needs-you list. You can start a new session in any project the PC knows about, on any account. A project exists once it has had one session on the PC or you have added its folder on the board; after that, it shows on the phone with nothing more to set up.
Reaching a PC session from the phone needs Claude's own Remote Control, set up per session.
An installable app that opens straight to your board.
Every project on the PC is one tap away on the phone.

changes.alt: Two phone screens: the board listing plunderspell and EdensProjectRouter with account badges, and a live terminal asking to allow an edit with Esc, up, down and Enter keys below
changes.caption: Mock-up of the phone app: the board, then a live session.

changes: new
Pairing your phone, once
Scan one code on the PC, and the phone remembers it for good.

The PC app shows a QR code that works for five minutes and only once. Scanning it with the phone app swaps a private key that the phone keeps, and every later request carries it. The PC refuses anything without a paired key, and you can unpair a phone from the PC at any time. How the phone reaches the PC when you are away from home is the first question in Your choices below, "How should the phone reach the PC away from home?"
Your phone has no way to connect to your PC.
A one-time pairing with a key only your phone holds.
After one scan the phone simply connects, with nothing to type.

changes.alt: PC showing a pairing QR code, then your one-time scan, then the phone saying paired and that it remembers the PC
changes.caption: Pairing: the orange step is the only thing you do.

changes: new
How you get the apps
GitHub builds both installers for you; you download them.

GitHub Actions (GitHub's free build machines) builds EdensRouter-Setup.exe on a Windows machine and EdensRouter.apk on a Linux machine every time the branch changes, so nothing needs installing on your PC to build them. Two one-time warnings are expected because the apps are not signed with a paid certificate: Windows SmartScreen asks you to click More info, then Run anyway, and Android asks you to allow installs from your browser or file app. Signing certificates cost money, so they stay out of the prototype.
There are no installers to download yet.
Two installers you download from GitHub.
Install once on each device, then updates are a new download.
new
Milestones you can check
Six steps, each with a test you can run yourself.

There are six, in this order. The approved plan: you send your answers and the approval, using Copy my reply. The desktop app: you install EdensRouter-Setup.exe, see sessions from all four of your accounts grouped by project, and start and resume a session inside the app. The Visual view: in a live session, a question Claude asks shows as a card, tapping an answer moves the terminal on, and a page Claude writes shows in the conversation. The account handoff: a session started on Main resumes on Work with its earlier messages visible. I run this copy test before building the account router, because the router depends on the copy working. The phone at home: you pair the phone on home Wi-Fi, answer a question in the Visual view on the phone, and see the PC's terminal move on. The phone away from home: the same test with the phone on mobile data. After these six, daily use follows, as in the project roadmap, docs/2-roadmap/Roadmap.md.
The roadmap stops at a PC-only prototype.
A roadmap with desktop, handoff and phone milestones.
You can tell exactly how far along it is.
new
Risks and unknowns
What could sink or slow the plan, and which milestone checks it.

Turning a tap into key presses depends on how Claude's terminal lays out each question, and that layout can change between Claude versions. The Visual view milestone tests it first. If it proves fragile, the fallback is Claude's app protocol. That is the second answer to the question "How should the Visual view talk to Claude?" Moving a transcript between accounts has not been tried, because it needs two signed-in accounts and only your PC has them. If Claude refuses to resume a copied session, the fallback is a new session on the other account that starts with a summary of the old one. The handoff milestone shows which of those two happens. Spotting the usage-limit message relies on Claude's wording, which can change; I will start by looking for that exact message text, and the same handoff test checks it. The PC must be on and awake for the phone to reach it; waking a sleeping PC remotely is not in this plan. The session file layout was read on Linux, not Windows, and the desktop-app test checks it on your PC. Using several accounts is between you and Anthropic, so check that it fits their terms; the router keeps each account's sign-in separate and never pools them. A phone notification needs the app's link to stay open in the background, which uses some battery; the phone-at-home test measures how much.
Nothing is measured yet.
A named check for each unknown.
You see the risks before any code exists.
choices: How should the Visual view talk to Claude?
Real terminal, Visual view read from the transcript
Claude runs in its normal terminal. The Visual view is drawn from the transcript file, and your taps are typed in as keys. You keep the full terminal with every command, and both views work at once.

choices.alt: Diagram of the terminal and Visual view fed by one live session
choices.caption: Real terminal, Visual view from the transcript.

choices: The router runs Claude the way the Claude apps do, through its message stream (the protocol Anthropic's Agent SDK uses; the SDK is its toolkit for building on Claude). Questions and permissions arrive as exact data, so answers never depend on screen layout. The terminal view becomes a plain text replay rather than the live terminal, so menus such as /model are not there.

The real terminal with a transcript-drawn Visual view is the only way to keep the terminal you asked for alongside the Visual view. Claude's app protocol is the fallback if the Visual view milestone shows that turning a tap into key presses is unreliable.
How should the phone reach the PC away from home?

A free private network app for personal use, built on open-source WireGuard. You install it on the PC and the phone and sign in once; after that the phone reaches the PC from anywhere, encrypted, with no router settings.
Nothing extra to install, but the phone only works when it is on the same Wi-Fi as the PC.
Free and works anywhere, but needs a Cloudflare account and a web domain you own, and your traffic passes through Cloudflare.
Tailscale is the only one that works anywhere with no account or domain to manage, and its one-time sign-in is the only extra step. Home Wi-Fi keeps working either way.
Which account should a session use?
Each project opens on its last-used account; when that account is out of usage, one tap moves it to one with room.
You pick the account whenever you start or resume a session.
You set an account per project once, and it never moves on its own.
Automatic matches your goal of never switching accounts, and still asks before moving a conversation.
What should both apps be built with?

Electron makes the Windows .exe and Capacitor wraps the same screens into an Android APK, so one set of screens serves both. Both are open source, and I can test all of it on my side. The .exe is large, roughly 100 MB, because Electron bundles its own browser.
Electron and a native Android app
The phone app is written separately in Kotlin, Android's own language. It feels the most native, but every screen is built twice.
One open-source toolkit for both, with a .exe around ten times smaller. Its terminal support and Android builds are less proven, so it reaches you less tested.
Electron and Capacitor build every screen once and use the best-tested terminal libraries, which matters most for a prototype.
Which of the seven ADHD and autism features come in the first build?
The Needs-you list, focus card, Now strip, Why line and calm scrolling come with the Visual view. The Where-you-were card and Pages shelf follow straight after the Visual view milestone passes.
Everything arrives together, and the first build reaches you later.
Starting with the core five gets the features that cut the most noise into your hands sooner; the Where-you-were card and Pages shelf build on them.

wrapup.summary: A Windows app and an Android app that each show every session as the real terminal and as a Visual view like the Claude app, across all your accounts, designed around ADHD and autism.
wrapup.changing: Nothing is built yet. This plan turns the first design into an installable Windows .exe and an Android APK. Both devices get a Terminal view and a Visual view of the same live session. It adds seven features built for ADHD and autism, any number of accounts with an account router, and phone pairing.
